claims.text: HEA strength and hardness are primarily governed by lattice distortion caused by the random distribution of dissimilarly sized atoms.
Controlled heat treatments can induce uniform, coherent nanoprecipitates in the proposed HEA variants.
Uniform, coherent nanoprecipitates provide additional dislocation-pinning and strengthening.
Equiatomic HEAs can exist as FCC or BCC single-solid-solution structures.
Varying constituent atomic-size differences can produce HEA variants with relatively high and low lattice distortion.
Dislocation-mediated plastic deformation dominates from room temperature to approximately 400°C in the proposed alloys.
Random mixing of elements with different atomic radii creates severe local lattice strain and variation in interatomic distances.
Local lattice strain raises the energy barrier for dislocation movement and produces solid-solution strengthening.
HEAs with greater atomic-size mismatch will exhibit higher hardness and yield strength than a low-distortion, single-phase baseline.
HEAs containing a high density of coherent nanoprecipitates will exhibit higher hardness and yield strength than an unprecipitated baseline.
Hardness and yield strength should scale with the degree of atomic misfit.
Hardness and yield strength should scale with coherent-precipitate volume fraction.
The proposed mechanism applies only while dislocation motion dominates and the microstructure remains stable without excessive segregation or brittle intermetallic formation.
At sufficiently high temperature, grain-boundary-dominated deformation or microstructural instability can invalidate the proposed strengthening mechanism.
The relative quantitative contributions of lattice-distortion strengthening and coherent-precipitate strengthening vary among HEA systems and processing routes.
A lack of statistically significant hardness and yield-strength improvement in the high-distortion or precipitate-strengthened material relative to the baseline would falsify the proposed mechanism.
